function.name: cmd_controller_execute
function.description: Executes a system-level command using os.system() on Windows operating systems. It can execute single or multiple commands chained with '&&'. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

command.description: The system command to be executed. To execute multiple commands, separate them with '&&'. For example, 'dir && echo done'.

unit.description: The unit of measurement for the command execution time, such as 'seconds' or 'milliseconds'

message.reasoning: The user wants to set a timer for 10 seconds using the timeout command. They say "You should use timeout 10." So they want to run a command that will wait for 10 seconds. On Windows, the timeout command is used like "timeout /t 10". But they specifically say "timeout 10". That might be a Linux command? Actually, "timeout" is a Linux command that runs a command with a time limit. But "timeout 10" alone would just exit after 10 seconds? In Linux, "timeout 10" will run the command "10"? No, "timeout" expects a duration and a command. If you just run "timeout 10", it will error because no command. But maybe they want to run "timeout 10" which will wait 10 seconds and then exit. But the correct usage is "timeout 10" on some shells? Actually, "timeout" is part of coreutils; usage: timeout DURATION COMMAND [ARG]... So "timeout 10" alone is incomplete. But maybe they want to run "timeout 10" which will wait 10 seconds and then exit. But we can just run "timeout 10" and it will exit after 10 seconds. But we need to use the function to execute a system command. So we call functions.cmd_controller_execute with command "timeout 10". We also specify unit "seconds" maybe. The function signature: command: string, unit?: "seconds" | "milliseconds". So we can pass unit "seconds". So we call the function.
